sentences.text: Sam, it.
Hey team, how's it going?
Yeah, good, thank you.
How are you?
I'm doing great, Doing really good.
Hi Trisha.
I assume he is.
Yeah, I think so.
I'll shoot him a message just to remind to make sure he's not zoned out on a, on a project or something.
Yeah, he'll see if he responds shortly.
Oh, there he is.
There he is.
Sorry for the time.
No worries.
I was just trying to get dialed in here.
Hey everybody.
Hi.
So thank you everyone for joining this call.
I'm Ahmed, I'm Capital A.
So we are representing Chris and Kriticli as our clients.
So just I'm just going to be here kicking off things and then I'm going to hand it over to you guys.
Just for you guys to know.
We have like this note taker in.
It just helps us track down any details or any important notes that come out of this call.
So just we'll keep things brief.
And Chris, would you like to introduce yourself and create a click to Claude.
And Claude, if you could do the same, that would be great.
Sure, yeah.
Well the guys have read the IM, so I'm sure they're well familiar, broadly speaking with QC.
But yes, I'm Chris, I'm the founder, set up QC 2008.
Previous to that I was the lead sort of technical person in a very high growth digital marketing agency.

Became the largest in the world, largest independent in the world that was acquired by Publicis and that was the point when I founded QC and obviously 20 years in the industry on the performance marketing side, that's our specialist area and that's certainly my background, where I'm coming from.
Well, thank you very much.
Just so I'll go my side.
Claude.
The last but we're basically a marketing tech.
Oh, sorry, I had someone try to call me while I was trying to do that.
Apologies.
So again CEO of Honor.
This is sort of my similar, I guess to use second time to the rodeo if you will.
Previously built an agency that I owned and kind of rolled up a bunch of different agencies and exited that business.
It was much more full service this time around.
Honor has a very, I guess specific focus.
So we're all digital really across healthcare and E commerce.
We have two subsidiary brands, one called of cost, one called Storia.
We're a bit unique, we're publicly traded, although small and mighty.

I got brought over by two family offices that were our first investors in the business or had really built the business initially and then we brought in some other institutional capital to the TABLE and basically my mandate has been to grow and scale this business and really with a very specific focus.

So we really, we say middle market, but you know, I think sometimes agency world doesn't love that, but really focus on growth brands and kind of both those two sectors and really focus on operating as much as humanly possible as like a SaaS business, even though we're an agency.
So we have a lot of different ways that we do that.
And so for us, obviously tech technology is at the forefront.
The company's, you know, 100% remote, with 60% of our workforce international, and we're very acquisitive.

So we're in the process of, you know, closing two acquisitions kind of in the pipeline, trying to do a third one before the end of the year, and really focused on going deep into kind of our two core verticals and really get very excited when there's, you know, businesses that have, I think, diversified client base and also sometimes unique technology that we can layer into what we're doing.
So that's, that's a super high level about us.
I'm sure there's a lot of questions about that which we can dive into.
Chris on the team has been with me for years.
He was at my previous agency group.
He helped us build Storia, our performance marketing business here.
He's now president of Honor and oversees both agencies.
And Trisha is on the call as well as our cfo.
She joined us in December.
Not from the agency world, but plenty of public company experience and audit world, which is kind of the world we live in.
And yeah, we're excited to learn a little bit more about the business.

You know, as I mentioned to Ahmed, when he originally reached out to us, you know, the, the company seemed a little bit small necessarily for what we would typically look at, but we're opportunistic, especially when we think something can have a fit.
And it seemed like there was a lot of fit between what we're doing at story and what you guys are doing.
So I think we're excited to learn a bit more about why you want to sell and then just maybe some high level details on kind of the business and, and, and, and when, how you see it.
Yeah, that sounds great and I can certainly see the fit there.
Claude, thank you.
That was really helpful.
Yeah.
If I go into a bit more detail about business.
So, you know, I mentioned I went to a very, very high growth, I guess early stage of my career.
So the business I was involved with before I founded qc, we were number one in the UK for words like SEO and search engine optimization.
So that was a business that grew incredibly quickly.
I came in employee 30 and we were sort of two and a half, 3,000 people.
A couple years later, lots of acquisitions of its own and it ultimately was acquired by Publicis.
And that's when I, when I founded qc.
What I learned going through that process was I think what really good performance marketing looks like on the organic and paid side.
And the value comes from that kind of middle, an enterprise market customer base.
So QC has always been in that area.
We sell ourselves very strongly on performance.
You'll see our strap line is passionate about performance and we really live and breathe that credo.

So we have an account development process which is entirely focused around making sure that we are delivering very high performance, organic or paid or unified strategies for our customers and then use that to land and expand the account amongst the senior stakeholders in there.
Predominantly UK focused.
We're 100% remote as well.
We do quarterly get togethers.
I think culture is very important.
We do invest quite a lot of time and effort in our team and making sure our team are right in terms of the size of the business.
You're quite right, Claude.
We absolutely could have driven this big business to be much larger earlier.

You'll be aware we have a system business, if you like, in the Corvette platform which we've developed over the last nine years, launched that business to market a year and a half ago, ticking into two years ago.
Now that's a AI based SaaS platform that unifies measurement across devices without the need of cookies or anything like that.
Massively improves your ability to deliver attribution, but also gives you automated value in paid media.
So that business we intend to invest in further, which is the reason for selling the services side of the business.
On the services side, we do also use a lot of technology that we've also developed in house.

Maybe slightly less hardcore than an enterprise grade AI platform, but we use tools such as Halo, for example, to provide integrated insights, allow us to understand what the most impactful opportunistic opportunities are in organic and paid search, tailor our strategies to those, tie them very tightly to building out forecasts, making sure that we can beat them, and essentially selling ourselves on the basis of roi.
We've been relatively flat over the last few years.

You know, we've not necessarily been growing that services side of the business and the rationale behind that is we've really been investing and trying to grow that other component of the organization, the Corvida software side of the business.
So that's really why we are where we are today.

My motivation is to make sure that QC gets an opportunity to be the brand it can be with a good cluster of like minded sister companies or as part of a wider organization that does things the right way, really delivers for customers.
I'd like to make sure that our team are part of a really important team community in the organization that ultimately acquires us.
I want to make sure that our customers continue to have best in class strategies and performance.
And certainly when Ahmed and the team brought you guys to our attention, it looked to me like honour would provide that kind of environment.
Awesome.
Awesome.
Super helpful in context and background.
So in terms of the organization today, just in terms of client mix and concentration being flat over the past few years, what is churn like for the organization?
What is new business like?
Where does that kind of come from?
You know?
And walk me through a little bit that, if you don't mind.
Yeah.
I might ask LA to cover off any specific numbers on that.
LA would like to jump in.
So LA heads up our finance team.
Good to meet you.
Laura.
Mute at the moment.
You're on mute.
You're on mute.
We're not able to hear you.
Hi.
Sorry about that.
Okay, so we've had quite a few clients.
We've got quite a few long term clients and a mix of multi year agreements and annual agreements.
We've had a couple of historic clients that have churned.
Last year a sizable client which initially started as a very small retainer.
They eventually turned after about four years but we are still acquiring and developing new clients.
Yeah.
So this is good movement on it at current year and we're seeing expansion on the current deals.
The other thing I would say about the client mix, you know, so you mentioned retail being an area of focus, but on our.
Certainly an area of focus with us.
So one of our larger customers is a major retailer in the beauty space and fashion.
They are actually B2C and B2B.
So they also supply into other businesses within that space.
We manage multinational for them.
We manage across some trade sites as well as those DTC consumer sites on the paid and organic side of things.
So quite an interesting complex customer has been with us for a good length of time.
We have some larger clients also in the mortgage space.
So lead generation into that mortgage space.
Those two clients represent what LA has called out, which is customers that have had a good long term relationship with us that we've had a lot of value to.
Similarly, we have a customer who is principally US based, who's been with us about a decade now.
So we like to try and build really deep relationships with customers.
But as LA pointed out, not all customers can, can stay forever.
For sure.
For sure.
And on average, like, what do you think, what would you say the service mix is between kind of paid versus organic and any other ancillary services?
Yeah, we wait slightly more towards organic.
I would say something a bit more like 60 40.
That's correct.
And in terms of ancillary services, we do an awful lot in the analytics side of things.
The technical specialisms, measurement, creation of dynamic reports, automation.
We're obviously adopters of using things like AI, agentic AI to help us with research.
We're very open book about all of that side of things, using it to make our time go further for our customers.
For the organic side, we take a look at inbound.
So for link development, we're quite advanced in the way that we look at that.
So we've restructured the way that we build our opportunities there using AI search as our basis.
So we know that there's a higher rate of Reference ability in AI overviews within top 100 results, but actually outside top, top three positions.

Which means for some of our customers who have very large competitors with much larger budgets than they have, it's a competitive edge for them to be able to deploy content and turn up in those overviews a fraction of the cost that it would have would have been otherwise for them.
So yeah, we try and mix it up in those ancillary spaces and make sure that we've got a good comprehensive coverage.
Most of our contracts were working usually to sort of either 6 or 12 month term strategy focus and contract terms.
And that's essentially the way that we look at it with our customers treating them like partners working as an extension of their team.
Some of our customers are incredibly reliant on our team.
Avi that makes very helpful, gives us a good context before I go any further.
Chris, any questions about that since we're talking a little bit of detail on the server side?
Yeah.
What's the pricing structure?
How do you model out the pricing?
Yeah, so for pretty much all of our customers, we'll allocate hours against the rate card and then that will be the bulk of their pricing.
For some of the ancillary stuff, there might be tooling costs in there and those are just essentially treated like license prices.
So it's a variable cost per month, but agreed upon rate cards.
Yeah.

And quite often the amount per month will be relatively standard and we might do reallocation either on a quarterly basis based on their peaks and troughs in their industry, or sometimes on a monthly basis.
We might reallocate time if we see critical priorities.
So I'll give you an example.
One of our customers, they're having significant server problems.
They know that they've got an issue there, they need our technical support.
And so we're reallocating more time away from inbound activity into technical SEO support for them, but netting out overall, broadly speaking, the same.
So we're typically trying to make it stable and predictable as much as we.
As we can in that billing structure.
So essentially some type of forecasted bucket of hours and then oftentimes a rate card against that.
Exactly.
And for some reason, if it balloons, then there's overages.
Yeah, that's right.
Thank you.
That's what I got called.
Christopher.
So.
And you, are you the main partner in the business?
Yeah.
Correct.
So it's just you.
Okay, cool.

And so your goal, I guess, just in theory, is to make sure a team lands in a great place, obviously culture fit, which is important for us too, and people who understand what's going on with the business, and then really to kind of transition your time to this other Martech platform that you're developing.
Is that correct?
Yeah, that's correct.
I want to make sure that the team are set up for success with the acquirer and that the acquirer is really getting what they.
What they expect.
For sure.
For sure.
Look, and I think at the end of the day, you know, I guess the biggest difference between us and like, maybe traditional private equity or some of the other strategics.
Right.
I think we're, we're interested in, in, you know, we, we're not.
So we're not.
Our time horizon, the way we think of things are not fundamentally linked to some sort of archaic structure or, you know, performance metrics or things like that.
Right.
So for us, it's, it's really more about.
Yeah.
Does this integrate?
Do, you know, do we think that, you know, the, the businesses can come together and that kind of keep us moving forwards in the overall strategy as much as everybody else?
Right, because I think the, you know, not to sell you.
Right.
But that's just, just generally speaking, you know, a big part of the reason we, you know, are a public company and growing the way we are and everything else.
Not just for the credibility and the audit perspective and all those elements, but also because, you know, every employee at the organization owns, you know, stock and what we're doing.
Right.
And are vested in the overall long term success of what we're trying to build.
And you know, having, since you've gone through a deal with the PO with this before or something like that, you know, the big holding companies really aren't growing these days.
Right.
But we, we think there's a lot of value to be captured between kind of 0 and 100, if you will.
And we're just the beginning of that journey.
Right.
So I think for us that's, you know, stability and, and knowing that we have something that we can build upon is, is, is, is almost the most important thing for us.
Yeah, that makes a lot of sense.
And I must say I agree with your strategy.
I think those larger holding companies, particularly with agentic AI at the moment, there's a sort of existential threat for many of them in terms of the way they operate.
It's a perfect opportunity for a really focused operator like yourselves, like QC to really make hay with it.
And I think it's going to be a really exciting couple of years from that perspective in the marketplace for sure.
So.
Yeah, I can see that.
Absolutely.
I like your point about culture.
I think culture fit is really critical.
I was interested in the fact, you know, I don't think there's as much coverage across the UK for you guys at the moment.
Is the UK a strategic market for you?
Is that something that is a deliberate part of the plan or is that just simply an opportunistic extra value?
No, so it absolutely is.

I mean, look, you know, and it's funny these days when I talk about this because I, you know, I started my professional career on the creative side and have become much more, I guess, the corporate finance guy over the years.
But I, I ride both lines still to this day and have both parts of my brain.
But you know, I think the biggest differentiator from the last business I, I built to kind of the team and what we're building here.
And look, every business has its challenges, its ups and downs, but the biggest differentiator is everything is thought of in terms of how do we maximize enterprise value, right?
Not just for ourselves, but for the employees, shareholders, what we're trying to do, right?
And so I mentioned a lot of things and you'll see a lot of our marketing materials kind of harp on those things, right?

Things like, you know, productized revenue or fixed pricing models or subscription like a service sort of operating right or having low client concentration or you know, in some ways, you know, sometimes people hear me say H and R block versus PwC or Warby Parker versus Luxottica in terms of who we're trying to be.
But it's a whole lot less about sector appeal and chasing big brand names and Cannes Lions award even though we're at Cannes lines every year.
And we have to have a presence from that perspective.
But it's much more about what are the things that create enterprise value.
Right.
And so I say all that in a long winded way to get back to your question that, you know, there is no secret that for us to have maximum enterprise value, it can't just be a North American strategy.
Right.
We need to have a presence in Europe and transparently, eventually, probably in the GCC and maybe even Asia.
Right.
The larger footprint we can have from a global positioning, the more value we have as a business.
Now, right now the focus has been, you know, and we have had some conversations.
I'll be transparent, you know, you know, there's a, there's a conversation we have going with a much larger agency in the UK that services predominantly US clients.
Right.
And our focus has been on brands that predominantly service U.S.
clients.
But it doesn't mean that we don't want to and don't see value in going the other direction.
And quite honestly, we've had international clients or clients that we started servicing in the US that we now work with their international teams.
Right.
So that is definitely part of the roadmap.

And I think what is interesting for us about this conversation, amongst many things, right, is that it seems like the client mix and size kind of fits and you know, and then again, obviously, I think if there is something to be done, it kind of gives us moving further that direction to start having that more international presence, which I think is important.
Yeah, that makes a lot of sense.
I think one of the major pieces of value that could be realized with QC is the quality of businesses that we work with, you know, particularly in Europe and the uk, that will be recognized.

You know, there's logos that, you know, we have case studies against and great credibility against and we get great reference ability against that in the UK and Europe are huge brands and fantastic brands.

And are these mostly your relationships that you brought in over the years of being in the industry or where, where, where did the client, current client relationships live and where has the new business typically come from in the past?
So all client relationships live with Jackie.
So she's mentioned in the im, she's our head, ultimately, she maintains and owns those relationships, if you like.
I offer kind of a technical leadership in.
So because I have 20 years in performance marketing and a very strong reputation, particularly in the U.K.
and Europe, but also in the U.S.
you know, I'm, I'm someone who is often consulted on certainly at the earlier stages when we're bringing new customers in.
We do bring customers in with inquiries that come in with events that maybe we've attended.
As I say, we've prioritized focusing in on Corviday over the last sort of three, four years.
And so typically in the course of discussing that, you know, services inquiries come out the back of that.
And so really that's, that's where that's come from.
We haven't been proactive in development there outside of that.
So yeah, Jackie owns the relationships and we pick up engagement just off the back of the credibility of the account.

People that have moved on who want to bring us in because they know we do a good job and because of our performance focus, they know that they're going to get what it says on the tin when they buy QC services and make sure that they get the right thing.
Totally.
Just a quick question, maybe dig a little deeper on that.
You're saying Jackie owns those relationships.
Is.
Yeah.
And, and it sounds like a lot of word of mouth.
Is that word of mouth based on like you have a quite a reputation, 20 years so on.
Is that word of mouth because of, you know, these people know you and have learned you and respect you over so, so long that they've done business and have succeeded that they keep coming back?
Or is, is, does Jackie, I guess we're asking, is there a sales operation that's in place in which, you know, outbound is, is converting even if that is organic, you know, through customer base?
Yeah, there is a sales operation and it's engaged through Jackie, you know, she owns the pitches and that side of things.
And I would also say, Chris, that, you know, QC itself has a reputation.
That's the important part.
We really do deliver excellent performance for customers.
And so those become case studies and those become the areas that are talked about as much as anything else.
Thank you.
Super helpful.
Look, I know we're coming up on the end of time.
I want to just open up obviously if you have any specific questions for us and if not, I'm happy to just jump in to how we think about process and maybe continuing the conversation.
Yeah.
Richard?
Yeah, My only question, I was interested in the Geographic piece, so I really appreciate you giving the background in that.
Cause the other would be just on the long term vision, I suppose.
Well, that's part of the question, right Is it medium or long term?
You talk about the value for shareholders and employees and obviously the team scale and the vision of what the end goal is.
Yeah, I think it's a good question.

I think I'll give you our answer and I'll be also realistic about, you know, depending on who the stakeholders are in the organization, there's different trajectories for what the, where they sit in terms of the value.
And so if I look at our original, you know, the, the two family officers who brought us into the deal in the long run, you know, in a lot of ways they, they, they function like market makers.
And so their goal is for us to obviously get a stock that's got volume and it's got trading and you know, there's all that.
Right.

But I think realistically what we're building as a team, it's, you know, a much more long term value that we're a long term plan that we're looking to capitalize, you know, both in kind of a two year roadmap and then kind of a five year roadmap.
Right.
And the two year roadmap is, look, we, we there, there's just the reality of being a public company which gives us a lot of opportunity, but also creates a lot of cost.
Right.

And so we need to grit scale and the scale is important to not only substantiate obviously the cost of being a public business, but also I think to create credibility and start creating some of that enterprise value.
Right.
And as I mentioned earlier, you know, there's a lot of things I learned from doing this the first time around, doing it a second time around, I would do different.
Right.
And one of those really specific strategies is being hyper focused in what we're doing in kind of performance digital marketing and going very deep within those strategies.
Right.
So I think near term success, acquisition wise, you know, it's very easy.
And I've been tempted myself to think, oh, we could add a new service, we can go horizontal, we can get into this space, we can get into that space.
But in reality, until we've kind of gotten the scale of, call it, you know, 50 to $100 million in revenue within one specific kind of offering, we really don't want to go horizontal.
Right.

And so from a business perspective, every acquisition that we're looking at right now is, is in one of our two verticals which with I would say 90% of them really being focused on anything kind of E commerce, retail, kind of just performance focused lead generation online.
Right.
So anywhere we can run or running advertisements or helping people within the walled gardens of the world.
Especially kind of, you know, in the size and scale of client we're looking for where we can kind of be acquiring those businesses.

Because at the end of the day, look, you can have a great agency, but in today's day and age, to grow faster than 20, 30%, which would be big growth for any agency on a year over year basis, you need to be getting that scale.
Right.
So that's kind of our near term focus, is really going deep into our existing verticals and then getting to the scale we can uplift to nasdaq.
Right.
Currently we're trading on otcqb.
It's a smaller market here in the US And a challenging one at that.
I look at it as the minor leagues in baseball, even though I'm not a baseball player.
And we're really focused on getting to the major leagues.
Right.
So that's, you know, and to do that again, the number is kind of $100 million plus is where we need to be in terms of kind of overall scope and size to get to that next level.
Right.
And then once we're on Nasdaq, I think there's a, it's a different roadmap.
Right.
The roadmap then becomes how are we continuing to scale within that ecosystem and then thinking about other ways to maximize enterprise value.
And that can be, and look, I'll be honest, I say this all the time.
I'm not one to have a five year plan.
I think in reality sometimes you plan and then life happens and there's agility and you have to adjust and things change.
But I think in reality there's one of two paths that happen in that five year roadmap.
One is, you know, we're, someone's coming around and saying, hey, we love what you're doing, we love your client set.
You really own this niche and you know, we want to buy you and that's a great day for everybody who's a shareholder in the business.
Right.
And that's fine.

And the other path is, look, we're growing, we're getting scale and you know, there's, there's, there's enough obviously opportunity for, for the people who have made, who have increase their share price value for being in the deal for years where they can start getting liquidity and you know, maybe we look more like a stagwell does at that period of time.
Right.
You know, so I think again, you know, I'm less focused on the long term exit.
I'm more focused on creating enterprise value along the way.
And I think that will create the opportunity that makes the most sense for the business in the long run.

But I'll tell you, like I said from the beginning, my focus is less chasing, you know, big blue chip stock, you know, big blue chip brands, and more building a resilient, highly diversified, you know, highly recurring, deep, I would just say fundamentally good business because I think that's what the markets want and that's what I think, you know, the world is transitioning to, especially with all the uncertainty and the shifts that we've seen over the years of maybe what's been the IPO market for many, for the past few years, so long winded way of answering it.
But that's, that's kind of how I see it.
No, I appreciate that.
Thank you.
Well, look, awesome.
I don't want to rush us and I'd like to have a follow up conversation.
I'll say that, you know, just, just you guys have a quick, you know, 30 seconds on how we usually look at this.
You know, we tend to be pretty upfront and try to, you know, as I say, rip the band aid off up front because everyone's time is precious, right.
And you know, kind of say, hey, this is how we're thinking about it.
This is what an economic deal could look like.

And, and have those conversations and assuming we can, you know, get to a place where that makes sense, then we kind of roll up the sleeves and invest the time and you know, fly across the world and sit down for dinners and really make sure that the culture and all those other things come together.
Because I tell you, I've, you know, years ago I did it the other way around.
And it's very fun how much time you could spend and waste before actually getting to the brass tacks.
But I'll tell you, at a high level, I think this is, you know, the conversation has been interesting.
I think we're interested in moving it forward.
As I said, let us, I would let us take us internally, think of any follow up questions we'd come back to you with at a high level.
And then maybe a little more financial information that we received today.
And then I think we would, our goal would be a turnaround, just, hey, this is how we're thinking of it.
Is this something you're interested in?
And then if yes, then we try to move to an loi and then, you know, move the process forward from there.
That sounds great, Claude.
Absolutely.
And it's been a delight to meet you and Chris and Tricia as well.
So, you know, if everyone's got the same quality, then it's going to be fantastic to have a lunch further down the line.
Absolutely.
Absolutely.
Well, I appreciate the time today, Ahmed.
Thank you for tracking us down and making this happen.
And we're looking forward to continuing the conversation.
Sounds great.
Okay, Have a great.
Thank you, everybody.

- ONAR, led by Claude Zdanow, is actively pursuing international expansion, targeting UK/Europe for increased enterprise value prior to moving into GCC and Asia markets.  
- Queryclick specializes in performance marketing with a service mix of 60% organic and 40% paid search, presenting significant insights through their proprietary technology, including the Halo tool.  
- The ONAR team aims to achieve $50-100 million in revenue to support a NASDAQ uplisting, underlining the need for strategic acquisitions to reach this scale.  
- Queryclick has maintained long-term client relationships, with notable clients in the beauty and fashion sector as well as lead generation for the mortgage industry.  
- ONAR's strategy emphasizes avoiding horizontal expansion until they establish revenue scale, specifically focusing on healthcare and e-commerce for digital marketing acquisitions.  
- Christopher mentioned that retention rates are strong, though some churn has occurred with historical clients, indicating areas for improvement in client engagement.  
- Claude outlined an upfront economic discussion approach to acquisition, emphasizing the importance of financial insight before deeper cultural assessments and due diligence processes.  
- The meeting concluded with a commitment from ONAR to internally review Queryclick’s opportunity and propose an economic framework for a potential acquisition.  
- Christopher expressed optimism about a cultural fit between Query
summary.short_summary: Christopher Liversidge emphasized Queryclick's development of the AI-based Corvida platform, which has been operational for 1.5-2 years, as a key reason for considering acquisition. ONAR, led by Claude Zdanow, is pursuing international expansion, primarily targeting the UK and Europe to enhance its enterprise value before entering GCC and Asia markets.
